questions.question: What is the primary definition of data collection?
options: The process of deleting unnecessary files from a computer
The systematic process of gathering and measuring information on targeted variables
The graphical representation of mathematical formulas
The method of turning hardware on and off

questions.question: Which of the following best describes qualitative data?
options: Data that can be measured with numbers
Data that describes qualities, characteristics, or categories
Data that is strictly formatted in SQL databases
Data that represents continuous numerical variables

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of quantitative data?
options: The color of a car
The texture of a fabric
The temperature outside in degrees Celsius
The type of cuisine a restaurant serves

questions.question: Why is ethical data collection important?
options: To ensure data uses up less storage space
To maximize the cost of data analysis
To protect individual privacy and prevent misuse of personal information
To make data completely unreadable by competitors

questions.question: What is 'sampling' in the context of data collection?
options: Selecting a representative subset of a population to make observations
Listening to audio recordings to extract data
Deleting every second row in a dataset
Creating a chart to show data distribution

questions.question: Which method is commonly used to collect structured feedback from a large group of people?
options: Deep-dive personal interviews
Surveys and questionnaires
Direct physical observation
Reading historical textbooks

questions.question: What is selection bias in data collection?
options: When the data sample is not representative of the true population
When the database crashes during collection
When data is collected too quickly
When all respondents give the exact same answer

questions.question: Which of the following is considered an observational method of data collection?
options: Counting the number of cars passing an intersection
Asking customers to fill out a feedback form
Downloading a pre-made CSV from the internet
Running a controlled chemistry experiment

questions.question: What does GIGO stand for in data science?
options: Gather In, Gather Out
Graphs In, Graphics Out
Garbage In, Garbage Out
Great Information, Great Output

questions.question: Why might an organization choose to collect data?
options: To make uninformed decisions
To increase their server maintenance costs
To discover patterns, answer questions, and test hypotheses
To avoid using computers entirely

questions.question: What is primary data?
options: Data that is collected by someone else for a different purpose
Data collected firsthand by the researcher for their specific project
Data that is over ten years old
Data that only contains numbers

questions.question: Which of the following is a source of secondary data?
options: Conducting a new survey in a shopping mall
Recording the temperature outside your window
Using a government census report published online
Interviewing a local business owner

questions.question: What is a major advantage of using secondary data?
options: It is always 100% accurate and unbiased
It is usually faster and cheaper to obtain than primary data
It perfectly matches the exact needs of your specific, unique project
It requires no cleaning or preparation

questions.question: What is an API (Application Programming Interface) in the context of data sources?
options: A piece of hardware that stores hard drives
A manual book of printed data tables
A software bridge that allows applications to fetch data from web servers dynamically
A tool used to draw bar charts

questions.question: What is 'web scraping'?
options: Physically cleaning a computer monitor
An automated method used to extract large amounts of data from websites
Deleting old websites from the internet
Writing new code for a web page

questions.question: Which of the following is an internal data source for a retail company?
options: A competitor's public pricing list
National economic inflation rates
The company's own sales transaction database
A public dataset on global weather

questions.question: What is 'open data'?
options: Data that is highly classified by the government
Data that is freely available to everyone to use and republish
Data that contains viruses
Data that is currently being downloaded

questions.question: Why must a researcher evaluate secondary data carefully?
options: Because it might have been collected using flawed methods or for a biased purpose
Because it is illegal to use secondary data
Because it will crash their computer
Because secondary data is always stored in an unreadable format

questions.question: Which collection method generates primary, qualitative data?
options: A thermometer recording temperature every hour
A focus group discussing their feelings about a new product
Downloading a stock market history dataset
Counting foot traffic using an automated turnstile

questions.question: Which data source would provide the most reliable demographic data for an entire country?
options: A poll on a social media influencer's page
A random survey of 10 people in one city
The official national census
A blog post about population estimates

questions.question: What does CSV stand for?
options: Computer Saved Variables
Comma-Separated Values
Common System Vector
Coded Structural Vision

questions.question: What is the primary structural characteristic of a CSV file?
options: It uses hierarchical nested tags
It organizes data in a tabular format using a specific delimiter, usually a comma
It stores data as images of text
It requires Microsoft Word to open

questions.question: What does JSON stand for?
options: JavaScript Object Notation
Java System Operation Node
Joint Standard Objective Network
Joined String Orientation Number

questions.question: How is data formatted in a JSON file?
options: As rows and columns with commas
Using tags like <name>John</name>
As key-value pairs, often nested, like {"name": "John"}
As a binary stream of 1s and 0s

questions.question: What is the main difference between an Excel (.xlsx) file and a CSV file?
options: CSV files support multiple sheets and formulas; Excel files do not
Excel files can save formatting, formulas, and multiple sheets; CSV is plain text only
CSV files are proprietary; Excel is open-source
Excel files can only store numbers; CSV can store text

questions.question: Which data format relies on tags to structure data, similar to HTML?
options: CSV
JSON
XML
TSV

questions.question: What type of data is a traditional SQL database best suited for?
options: Highly structured relational data in tables
Unstructured audio files
Nested, deeply complex JSON documents
Raw image pixels

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of unstructured data?
options: An Excel spreadsheet of employee salaries
A relational database of customer orders
A folder full of raw video files and text emails
A CSV file containing stock prices

questions.question: Why is JSON widely used in modern web APIs?
options: It is the only format computers understand
It is lightweight, easy for humans to read, and easily parsed by web languages like JavaScript
It automatically creates bar charts in the browser
It compresses data to take up zero storage space

questions.question: What does a TSV file use to separate data fields?
options: Commas
Colons
Tabs
Semicolons

questions.question: If you open a CSV file in a plain text editor, what will you see?
options: A fully formatted grid with colored cells
Lines of text where values are separated by commas
Unreadable binary code
A series of pie charts

questions.question: Which format is considered 'semi-structured'?
options: A standard SQL database table
A JSON file containing varied nested objects
A raw audio recording
A completely filled CSV file

questions.question: What is a 'delimiter' in data formats?
options: A character used to separate different values or fields in plain text files
A tool used to delete files
A mathematical function used to limit file size
The header row of a table

questions.question: Which data format would be best for transferring a massive, flat table of 10 million rows across systems efficiently?
options: Microsoft Word Document
CSV
XML
JPEG

questions.question: In JSON, what symbols are used to denote an array (a list of items)?
options: Curly braces { }
Parentheses ( )
Square brackets [ ]
Angle brackets < >

questions.question: What does a 'missing value' refer to in a dataset?
options: A value that is too large to display
An empty or null entry where data was expected but not recorded
A value that is statistically insignificant
A number that is negative

questions.question: Which of these is a common representation of a missing value in programming and databases?
options: NaN (Not a Number) or NULL
infinity
Done

questions.question: What is the primary risk of ignoring missing values in a dataset during analysis?
options: It will make the dataset too small
It can lead to biased models, skewed statistics, and incorrect conclusions
It will automatically delete the entire file
It will convert all numbers to text

questions.question: If a respondent skips a survey question about income because they find it too sensitive, this missing data is likely:
options: Missing Completely at Random (MCAR)
Missing Not at Random (MNAR)
A system error
Not considered missing data

questions.question: What does MCAR mean regarding missing data?
options: Missing Completely at Random; the missingness has no relationship with any data values
Multiple Categories Are Random
Machine Calculated Average Result
Missing Cars And Roads

questions.question: What is 'listwise deletion' (dropping rows)?
options: Filling in missing values with the mean
Removing the entire row/record if it contains any missing value
Deleting the entire dataset and starting over
Dropping the column that has missing values

questions.question: When is it generally acceptable to drop rows with missing values?
options: When the missing values make up 90% of the dataset
When the dataset is very large and the missing values account for a tiny, random fraction
When you don't know how to code an imputation
Always, it is the only correct method

questions.question: What is 'imputation' in data science?
options: The process of deleting missing values
The process of replacing missing data with substituted values, like the mean or median
The process of extracting data from a web page
The process of encrypting data

questions.question: If you have a column with a few missing values and severe outliers, which imputation method is safest?
options: Mean imputation
Median imputation
Dropping all columns
Replacing with zeros

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a common reason for missing data?
options: Human error during manual data entry
A sensor going offline for a few hours
The data successfully passing all validation checks
A user refusing to answer a specific survey question

questions.question: What is data cleaning?
options: Physically wiping down servers
The process of fixing or removing incorrect, corrupted, incorrectly formatted, duplicate, or incomplete data
Hiding data from unauthorized users
Sorting data from highest to lowest

questions.question: What does 'deduplication' mean?
options: Copying the data so there is a backup
Multiplying all values by two
Identifying and removing exact duplicate records from a dataset
Splitting one column into two

questions.question: Why is standardizing text data (e.g., converting all text to lowercase) an important cleaning step?
options: Because computers view 'Apple' and 'apple' as two entirely different distinct values
Because uppercase letters take up more memory
Because lowercase data is faster to download
Because standardizing text automatically fixes typos

questions.question: If a 'Date' column contains '12/01/2023', '2023-12-01', and 'Dec 1st 2023', what data cleaning step is required?
options: Deduplication
Format standardization to a single datetime format
Imputation
Dropping the column

questions.question: What is an 'outlier' in a dataset?
options: A data point that perfectly matches the mean
A data point that differs significantly from other observations
A value that is missing
A duplicate record

questions.question: If a column supposed to contain ages has a value of '999', what does this likely represent?
options: A very old person
A correct measurement
An error or a placeholder code for a missing/invalid value
The median of the dataset

questions.question: What is 'trimming whitespace'?
options: Removing spaces at the beginning and end of a text string
Deleting empty rows
Changing the background color of a graph to black
Removing missing values

questions.question: In a time series dataset (like daily weather), what does 'forward fill' imputation do?
options: Fills the missing value with the overall mean
Takes the last known value and carries it forward to fill the missing gap
Uses the next available future value to fill the gap
Deletes the missing day completely

questions.question: What does data type casting involve?
options: Throwing away unnecessary data
Converting data from one type to another, such as converting a 'string' of "123" into an 'integer' 123
Creating a duplicate dataset
Encrypting a database

questions.question: If a dataset has a column 'Customer_ID' with 10,000 unique rows, but 5 rows have identical IDs and identical information, what should you do?
options: Change the IDs randomly
Drop all 10,000 rows
Keep them, duplicates don't matter
Remove the duplicates to ensure data integrity

questions.question: Why would you remove irrelevant columns during data cleaning?
options: To make the dataset run slower
To reduce noise and save memory if the column does not contribute to your specific analysis
To intentionally lose data
Because datasets can only have 10 columns

questions.question: How can typo errors in categorical data (e.g., 'NY', 'N.Y.', 'New York') affect analysis?
options: It makes the analysis 3 times more accurate
The system will treat them as three separate categories, splitting the data incorrectly
It will crash the computer
Typographical errors have no effect on data analysis

questions.question: What is a 'sanity check' in data cleaning?
options: Running the data through an antivirus
A quick logical test, such as ensuring all 'Ages' are between 0 and 120
Testing the computer's RAM
Checking if the internet connection is stable

questions.question: Which imputation method is best for a column containing categorical data like 'City'?
options: Mean imputation
Median imputation
Mode (most frequent value) imputation
Zero imputation

questions.question: Data cleaning is usually estimated to take up what percentage of a data scientist's time?
What defines a 'clean dataset' ready for analysis?
options: It has no missing values, no duplicates, standardized formats, and correct data types
It has been printed on white paper
It contains only numbers
It is saved as a PDF

questions.question: According to 'Tidy Data' principles, what should each row represent?
options: A single variable
A single observation or record
The summary statistics of the dataset
A completely random set of numbers

questions.question: According to 'Tidy Data' principles, what should each column represent?
options: A single observation
A single variable or feature
A duplicate of the row
A random identifier

questions.question: What does data normalization or scaling achieve?
options: It changes all text to numbers
It adjusts the values of numeric columns to a common scale without distorting differences in the ranges of values
It encrypts the dataset
It removes all zeros from the data

questions.question: Why do we use One-Hot Encoding?
options: To heat up the computer processor
To convert categorical text variables into a binary numeric format (1s and 0s) for machine learning models
To merge two datasets together
To sort a column alphabetically

questions.question: If you have a column for 'Size' with values 'Small', 'Medium', 'Large', what type of encoding is most appropriate?
options: Label Encoding (e.g., 1, 2, 3), because there is an inherent order
Dropping the column
Leaving it as text
Replacing them with random numbers

questions.question: What is 'Feature Engineering' in dataset preparation?
options: Building a hardware feature
Creating new, useful columns (features) based on existing data to improve analysis
Deleting all columns
Drawing diagrams of the database

questions.question: If you have a 'Date of Birth' column, a feature engineering step might be to:
options: Delete the column
Calculate and create a new 'Current Age' column
Change all birth dates to today's date
Convert the date to a currency

questions.question: What is a Data Dictionary?
options: A book that translates foreign languages
A document describing the contents, format, meaning, and structure of the elements in a dataset
A software program that automatically cleans data
An alphabetical list of all words in a CSV file

questions.question: Why do data scientists often split a clean dataset into a 'training set' and a 'test set'?
options: To fit the data on a smaller USB drive
To train a machine learning model on one portion and evaluate its true performance on the unseen portion
To have a backup copy in case one breaks
Because databases have a row limit

questions.question: What is the primary use of a line chart?
options: To show the parts of a whole
To display trends or changes in data over continuous time intervals
To show correlation between two unrelated variables
To display the distribution of a single category

questions.question: On a standard time-series line chart, what does the horizontal X-axis represent?
options: The measured value or quantity
The categories being compared
Chronological time (e.g., days, months, years)
The cumulative total

questions.question: What does a downward sloping line on a line chart indicate?
options: An increasing trend
A decreasing trend over time
No change over time
A formatting error

questions.question: Why are the data points in a line chart connected by a line?
options: To make it look like a bar chart
To imply a continuous progression or transition between the measured data points
To trap the data inside a shape
To measure the area under the points

questions.question: When is it appropriate to use multiple lines on a single line chart?
options: To compare the trends of multiple distinct categories over the same time period
When you only have one variable
When the data represents disjointed, unrelated categories
Never, a line chart can only have one line

questions.question: In a line chart, what does a flat, horizontal line signify?
options: Rapid growth
Severe decline
Stagnation or no change in the value over that time period
An outlier in the data

questions.question: Which of the following datasets is best visualized with a line chart?
options: The favorite colors of 100 students
The monthly sales revenue of a store over the last 5 years
The height versus the weight of a group of dogs
The market share of three different smartphone brands today

questions.question: What is a risk of having too many lines plotted on a single line chart?
options: The lines will become bar charts
It becomes a 'spaghetti chart', making it cluttered and impossible to read
The axes will disappear
The data will become correlated automatically

questions.question: If a line chart shows distinct, repeating peaks every December, what is this pattern called?
options: An outlier
A negative trend
Seasonality
A flatline

questions.question: Why is it generally bad practice to use a line chart for categorical data (e.g., Apples, Bananas, Oranges on the X-axis)?
options: Because the lines are too thin to see
Because connecting categorical variables implies a sequential transition that doesn't exist
Because categorical data has no numbers
Because it will look like a pie chart

questions.question: What is the primary use of a bar chart?
options: To show trends over continuous time
To compare quantities or frequencies across different distinct categories
To plot geospatial coordinates
To find outliers in continuous numerical data

questions.question: In a vertical bar chart (column chart), what determines the value of a category?
options: The width of the bar
The color of the bar
The height of the bar reaching the Y-axis
The distance between bars

questions.question: When is a horizontal bar chart usually preferred over a vertical one?
options: When the category names are very long and need space to be readable
When there is only one category
When tracking time-series data
When showing parts of a whole

questions.question: What is a 'grouped' or 'clustered' bar chart?
options: A chart where all bars are combined into one giant bar
A chart placing bars of different sub-categories side-by-side for each main category group
A chart that only uses circles
A line chart disguised as a bar chart

questions.question: What is a 'stacked' bar chart used for?
options: Showing the total size of categories while also showing the proportional breakdown of sub-groups within them
Hiding negative numbers
Plotting relationships between two continuous variables
Showing seasonal trends over time

questions.question: Why must the numerical axis of a bar chart almost always start at zero?
options: To make the chart taller
To prevent visual distortion, as bar charts use length to represent proportion; truncating the axis exaggerates differences
Because negative numbers don't exist in data
It is just a stylistic choice with no mathematical reason

questions.question: What is a common best practice for ordering bars in a standard bar chart (unless there is an inherent order like dates or age groups)?
options: Randomly order them
Order them alphabetically to make them look jagged
Sort them sequentially by value (ascending or descending) to make comparison easier
Sort them by the length of the category name

questions.question: Which of these is the main difference between a Bar Chart and a Histogram?
options: Histograms show trends over time; bar charts show correlation
Bar charts show distinct categories with gaps between bars; Histograms show continuous numerical distributions with no gaps
Histograms only use lines
There is no difference; they are the exact same thing

questions.question: Why are 3D effects on bar charts generally considered a bad design choice?
options: They use up too much ink when printing
They distort the perspective, making it difficult to accurately align the top of the bar with the axis values
They make the chart look too modern
They turn the bar chart into a scatter plot

questions.question: If you want to show the number of cars sold by 5 different companies last month, which chart is best?
options: Line chart
Scatter plot
Bar chart
Pie chart

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of a scatter plot?
options: To show the relationship or correlation between two continuous numeric variables
To show the frequency of a single categorical variable
To display a sequential time series
To show parts of a whole

questions.question: In a scatter plot, how is a single data point represented?
options: By a vertical bar
By a slice of a circle
By a single dot placed at the intersection of its X and Y axis values
By a line connecting it to the origin

questions.question: If the dots on a scatter plot generally form a line sloping upwards from left to right, this indicates:
options: A negative correlation
A positive correlation
No correlation
An error in the data

questions.question: If the dots on a scatter plot form a line sloping downwards from left to right, this indicates:
options: A positive correlation
A negative correlation
A zero correlation
A categorical relationship

questions.question: What does a scatter plot look like when there is no correlation between the two variables?
options: A perfectly straight horizontal line
A perfectly straight vertical line
A random, scattered cloud of dots with no discernible pattern
A perfect circle

questions.question: On a scatter plot investigating cause and effect, where is the independent variable usually plotted?
options: On the vertical Y-axis
On the horizontal X-axis
As the color of the dot
As the size of the dot

questions.question: How are outliers visually identified on a scatter plot?
options: They are colored red automatically
They are points that lie far away from the general cluster or trend line of the other data points
They form a perfect straight line
They are placed on the axis lines

questions.question: What is a 'line of best fit' (or trendline) in a scatter plot?
options: A line that connects every single dot in chronological order
A straight or curved line drawn through the center of the data points that best represents the overall trend
The border around the chart area
The Y-axis line

questions.question: What is 'overplotting' in a scatter plot?
options: Making the axes too long
When too many data points overlap, creating a solid block of color and hiding the density of the data
Plotting data that doesn't belong
Drawing the line of best fit incorrectly

questions.question: If you add a third numerical variable to a scatter plot by changing the size of the dots, what is the resulting chart commonly called?
options: A Bubble Chart
A 3D Bar Chart
A Density Plot
A Stacked Scatter Plot
